narratives.name: Extending Kubernetes with KubeVirt for Unified Workload Management
narratives.description: How OpenShift Virtualization extends the Kubernetes platform to run VMs alongside containers on shared infrastructure.

narrativeContexts.context: OpenShift Virtualization extends the Kubernetes platform with KubeVirt operators to run VMs alongside containers, consolidating both workload types on a single infrastructure with unified management tooling.

The HyperConverged Operator deploys virt-controller, virt-handler, virt-api, and CDI as the foundational virtualization stack. Worker nodes require RHCOS with hardware virtualization extensions, while storage must support block volume mode and RWX access for live migration.

Organizations running dual virtualization and container stacks report 40-60% reduction in infrastructure costs after consolidation, with KVM-based virtualization delivering near-bare-metal performance validated through SPEC benchmarks.

Platform maturity for virtualization follows the same progression as container workloads but adds VM-specific gates at each state for operator health, storage compatibility, and live migration readiness.

narratives.name: Consolidating VM and Container Workloads on Kubernetes
narratives.description: Strategic context for adopting OpenShift Virtualization to unify VM and container workloads on a single platform.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations operating VM workloads on legacy virtualization platforms face growing infrastructure costs, operational fragmentation between VM and container stacks, and skills silos that slow modernization.

Consolidate VM and container workloads onto a single Kubernetes-native platform with enterprise-grade live migration, disaster recovery, performance tuning, and a structured migration path from legacy hypervisors.

Deploy OpenShift Virtualization with KubeVirt to run VMs alongside containers, configure Multus secondary networks and CSI-backed persistent storage, establish golden image pipelines, implement OADP-based backup, and migrate workloads from VMware, RHV, and OpenStack using the Migration Toolkit for Virtualization.

Unified infrastructure reduces costs and operational complexity, enables self-service VM provisioning through templates and instance types, delivers near-bare-metal performance via CPU pinning, NUMA awareness, and GPU passthrough, and provides a clear modernization path from VMs to containers.

narratives.description: Architecture and maturity progression of the KubeVirt operator stack across node configuration, operational validation, and performance tuning.

narrativeContexts.context: The virtualization infrastructure comprises the HyperConverged Operator, KubeVirt components (virt-controller, virt-handler, virt-api), and CDI, deployed on RHCOS worker nodes with hardware virtualization extensions.

HCO serves as the single entry point for deploying and reconciling all virtualization components. Worker nodes require bare metal or compatible cloud infrastructure with Intel VT-x or AMD-V extensions. The platform supports AMD64, ARM64, and IBM Z architectures with varying feature availability.

TLS certificates rotate automatically (daily for KubeVirt, every 15 days for CDI, yearly for MAC pool), eliminating manual certificate management. GPU passthrough and vGPU support enable AI/ML and rendering workloads with near-bare-metal performance.

Infrastructure maturity progresses from basic operator deployment through node configuration and operational validation to advanced optimization with GPU passthrough, NUMA awareness, and dedicated migration networks.

The QEMU guest agent provides guest OS information, enables filesystem freezing for consistent snapshots, and reports network interface details. OADP with kubevirt plugin supports both containerized applications and VMs for backup and restore.
VM lifecycle maturity progresses from template standardization through automated provisioning to governed operations with policy enforcement, backup automation, and compliance tracking.

narrativeContexts.context: VMs use native Kubernetes storage primitives with CDI enabling disk image import from HTTP endpoints, container registries, S3 object stores, and existing PVC clones.

Block volume mode provides significantly better performance than Filesystem mode for VM disks and is the default. RWX access mode is required for live migration, enabling multiple nodes to access the same persistent volume simultaneously.

CDI supports multiple cloning strategies (CSI volume cloning preferred, smart cloning, host-assisted fallback) with storage live migration available from OpenShift Virtualization 4.17 for rebalancing between storage providers.
VM storage maturity moves from basic provisioning through CDI-automated import and performance tuning to full integration with backup, snapshot, and disaster recovery workflows.

narratives.name: Pod and Secondary Network Connectivity for VMs
narratives.description: Network architecture progressing from pod network masquerade through Multus secondary networks to SR-IOV high-performance connectivity.

narrativeContexts.context: VMs connect to the default pod network via masquerade binding for basic SDN access, with secondary network attachment through Multus CNI enabling Linux bridge, OVN-Kubernetes, and SR-IOV connections.

OVN-Kubernetes localnet topology is recommended for exposing VMs to physical networks, while layer2 topology provides overlay networking preserving IP addresses across live migration. SR-IOV enables high-bandwidth, low-latency networking for performance-critical workloads including DPDK.

Hot-plug support allows adding and removing secondary NICs without stopping VMs. Dedicated migration networks minimize live migration impact on tenant workloads, preventing bandwidth contention during memory-state transfer.
VM networking maturity progresses from pod network connectivity through Multus secondary networks to SR-IOV high-performance networking and optimized multi-tenant network architectures.

activities.name: Install and Configure Virtualization Operator
activities.description: Deploy the OpenShift Virtualization operator stack and configure worker nodes for VM hosting.

narratives.name: Deploying the Virtualization Operator via OperatorHub
narratives.description: How to deploy the HyperConverged Operator, create the custom resource, and validate KubeVirt component health on worker nodes.

narrativeContexts.context: Deploy the HyperConverged Operator from OperatorHub, create the HyperConverged custom resource, and validate that all KubeVirt components are healthy on designated worker nodes.

Install the operator through OLM, configure the HyperConverged CR in the openshift-cnv namespace, validate node readiness by confirming RHCOS, hardware virtualization extensions, and KVM modules. Configure node labeling, storage classes, and the nmstate operator for network management. Verify virt-handler DaemonSet runs on all designated nodes and basic VM operations succeed.

Common mistakes include deploying on nodes without hardware virtualization extensions, which causes silent failures. Neglecting to configure storage classes before VM creation leads to PVC binding failures. Skipping SCCs review for virt-launcher pods creates security policy conflicts.

activities.name: Create and Manage VM Templates
activities.description: Design instance types, preferences, and golden images for standardized VM provisioning.

narratives.name: Building Golden Image Pipelines for Self-Service Provisioning
narratives.description: How to create instance types, configure CDI polling for golden image updates, and establish template governance with version tracking.

narrativeContexts.context: Define instance types for compute resource profiles, configure CDI for golden image polling, and establish template governance with version tracking and automated updates via OpenShift Pipelines.

Create VirtualMachineClusterInstancetype resources for cluster-wide profiles and configure CDI to poll container registries for Red Hat base images, or for custom golden images build a base VM, generalize it, and publish as a container disk. Automate golden image lifecycle with OpenShift Pipelines and GitOps for multi-cluster distribution, using the UEFI installer pipeline for Windows images.

Key pitfalls to avoid include not automating golden image updates, which leads to stale, unpatched base images. Creating too many instance types fragments standardization. Neglecting Windows golden image preparation with UEFI pipeline causes boot failures.

activities.name: Provision and Configure Virtual Machines
activities.description: Create, configure, and deploy VMs using templates, instance types, or manifests.

narratives.name: Creating VMs from Templates, Instance Types, and Manifests
narratives.description: How to provision VMs via the web console, instance types, or YAML manifests with storage, networking, and guest agent configuration.

narrativeContexts.context: Create VMs from templates via the web console, from instance types, or from VirtualMachine YAML manifests. Configure storage, networking, and guest agent, then validate boot and connectivity.

Select a template with an available boot source, customize resource allocations, attach storage volumes (boot disk from golden image, data disks as PVCs), and install the QEMU guest agent for guest OS visibility. Use virtctl CLI for VM-specific operations and enforce VM naming conventions (47 characters or fewer) for live migration compatibility.

Teams frequently encounter issues such as VM names exceeding 47 characters, which prevent live migration. Neglecting QEMU guest agent installation loses guest OS visibility and prevents consistent snapshots. Setting Filesystem volume mode instead of Block degrades performance significantly.

activities.name: Configure VM Networking
activities.description: Design and implement network connectivity for VMs across pod, secondary, and external networks.

narratives.name: Attaching VMs to Pod and Secondary Networks with Multus
narratives.description: How to configure pod network masquerade, Multus secondary networks with OVN-Kubernetes or Linux bridge, and SR-IOV for high-performance connectivity.

narrativeContexts.context: Configure pod network masquerade binding, establish Multus secondary networks with OVN-Kubernetes or Linux bridge topologies, deploy SR-IOV for high-performance workloads, and set up dedicated migration networks.

Define NetworkAttachmentDefinition resources for secondary networks, configure OVN-Kubernetes localnet topology with NNCP mapping to physical interfaces, and for SR-IOV install the operator with SriovNetworkNodePolicy for virtual functions. Enable hot-plug NIC support, configure external access via Routes or LoadBalancer Services, and align NIC placement with NUMA topology for optimal performance.

Critical risks in this area include choosing Filesystem-mode bridges when localnet topology would be more appropriate. Not configuring a dedicated migration network causes migration traffic to compete with production workloads. Misaligning SR-IOV NIC placement with NUMA topology degrades network performance by 10% or more.

activities.name: Configure VM Storage
activities.description: Design and implement storage architecture for VM persistent volumes, data import, and cloning.

narratives.name: Configuring CSI Storage Classes and CDI Data Import
narratives.description: How to configure storage classes with block volume mode, CDI for multi-source disk import, and RWX access for live migration support.

narrativeContexts.context: Define StorageClasses with block volume mode as default, configure CDI for data import from multiple sources, ensure RWX access mode for live migration, and validate CSI snapshot capabilities.

Create storage classes with block volume mode as default and configure DataVolume resources for declarative disk provisioning, with CDI selecting the most efficient cloning strategy (CSI cloning preferred, smart cloning, host-assisted fallback). Validate RWX access for live migration scenarios and configure VolumeSnapshotClass resources for snapshot and restore operations.

Frequent errors include using Filesystem volume mode instead of Block for VM disks, which reduces I/O performance significantly. Not configuring RWX access mode prevents live migration. Ignoring storage live migration capabilities from OpenShift Virtualization 4.17 misses rebalancing opportunities.

activities.name: Perform Live Migration
activities.description: Move running VMs between nodes without downtime for maintenance, balancing, or failure prevention.

narratives.name: Migrating Running VMs Between Nodes Without Downtime
narratives.description: How to initiate live migration via console, virtctl, or migration resources, configure dedicated migration networks, and manage PostCopy mode for large-memory VMs.

narrativeContexts.context: Initiate live migration through the console, virtctl CLI, or VirtualMachineInstanceMigration resources. Configure dedicated migration networks and manage CPU compatibility between nodes.

Verify shared storage (RWX access) and compatible CPUs on source and destination nodes, using PostCopy mode for large-memory VMs to reduce migration time. Configure a dedicated Multus network for migration traffic, and for planned maintenance cordon the node to trigger migration via the LiveMigrate eviction strategy.

Common mistakes include attempting migration without RWX storage, which fails silently. VM names exceeding 47 characters block migration. Not sizing the migration network for concurrent migrations causes bandwidth exhaustion and prolonged migration times.

activities.name: Configure Snapshots and Backups
activities.description: Establish VM snapshot capabilities and OADP-based backup and recovery procedures.

narratives.name: Protecting VM Data with OADP Snapshots and Backups
narratives.description: How to configure VolumeSnapshotClass resources, deploy OADP with kubevirt and openshift plugins, and establish backup schedules with retention policies.

narrativeContexts.context: Configure VolumeSnapshotClass resources for CSI snapshots, deploy OADP with kubevirt and openshift plugins, establish backup schedules with retention policies, and validate restore procedures through regular drills.

Install OADP with kubevirt and openshift plugins, configure VolumeSnapshotClass resources and Data Protection Application with backup storage location, and enable Data Mover for off-site backup relocation. Set backup schedules using Backup custom resources with retention specifications, and ensure QEMU guest agent is installed for filesystem freezing during online snapshots.

Key pitfalls to avoid include using OADP versions below 1.3 with OpenShift Virtualization 4.14+, which causes compatibility failures. Neglecting Data Mover configuration leaves backups without off-site protection. Skipping guest agent installation produces inconsistent snapshot data.

activities.name: Implement Disaster Recovery
activities.description: Deploy and configure cross-site DR infrastructure for VM workloads.

narratives.name: Implementing Metro-DR and Regional-DR for VM Workloads
narratives.description: How to select and deploy Metro-DR (synchronous, zero data loss) or Regional-DR (asynchronous, geographic separation) infrastructure with RHACM and ODF.

narrativeContexts.context: Select Metro-DR (synchronous, zero data loss) or Regional-DR (asynchronous, geographic separation) based on recovery objectives, deploy RHACM hub with ODF and DR operators, and validate failover/failback through testing.

Deploy RHACM on a hub cluster with ODF Multicluster Orchestrator, configure storage replication (synchronous for Metro-DR within 10ms RTT, asynchronous for Regional-DR), and create DRPolicy and DRPlacementControl resources. Configure hub recovery with a passive hub for orchestrator resilience, and for third-party storage use storage-level replication with OADP metadata-only backups.

Teams frequently encounter issues such as network latency exceeding 10ms RTT between sites, which disqualifies Metro-DR. Not configuring hub recovery leaves the DR orchestrator as a single point of failure. Skipping regular DR drills means untested procedures fail during actual events.

activities.name: Execute Workload Migration
activities.description: Migrate VMs from legacy virtualization platforms to OpenShift Virtualization using MTV.

narratives.name: Migrating Legacy VMs with the Migration Toolkit for Virtualization
narratives.description: How to install MTV, configure source providers, create migration plans with cold and warm strategies, and execute wave-based VM migrations.

narrativeContexts.context: Install MTV operator, configure source provider connections, create migration plans grouping VMs by dependency and strategy (cold vs warm), execute wave-by-wave migration, and validate migrated VMs.

Install MTV from OperatorHub, create provider connections to source platforms (VMware vSphere, RHV, OpenStack), and for VMware create the VDDK image and enable CBT for warm migration support. Create migration plans grouping VMs by dependency and criticality, execute cold migration for downtime-tolerant VMs and warm migration for critical workloads, and increase NFC service memory on ESXi hosts for migrations exceeding 10 VMs per host.

Practitioners should watch for not enabling CBT on VMware VMs, which prevents warm migration. Migrating more than 10 VMs per ESXi host without increasing NFC service memory causes timeout failures. Skipping post-migration performance validation allows latent issues to reach production.

activities.name: Configure Monitoring and Alerting
activities.description: Set up Prometheus metrics, alerting rules, and dashboards for VM observability.

narratives.name: Multi-Cluster VM Monitoring with Prometheus and RHACM
narratives.description: How to leverage the Prometheus monitoring stack for VM metrics, deploy node-exporter for guest OS visibility, and configure RHACM dashboards for multi-cluster monitoring.

narrativeContexts.context: Leverage the pre-installed Prometheus monitoring stack for default VM metrics, deploy node-exporter on VMs for guest OS metrics, create custom alerting rules, and aggregate multi-cluster metrics via RHACM.

Verify default virtualization metrics are scraped (vCPU, memory, network I/O, storage I/O) and deploy node-exporter on VMs requiring guest OS metrics. Define custom PromQL queries and alerting rules with PrometheusRule resources, and configure RHACM for multi-cluster VM monitoring.

Critical risks in this area include not deploying the QEMU guest agent, which prevents guest OS metrics from being reported. Creating alerting rules without associated runbooks leads to unactionable alerts. Neglecting project-scoped monitoring RBAC exposes metrics across teams.

activities.name: Implement Security Controls
activities.description: Configure RBAC, network policies, compliance scanning, and security hardening for VMs.

narratives.name: Enforcing VM Security with RBAC and Confidential Computing
narratives.description: How to define RBAC roles, deploy Compliance Operator scanning, implement network policies, and enable confidential computing for sensitive workloads.

narrativeContexts.context: Define RBAC roles for VM administrators, operators, and viewers. Deploy the Compliance Operator for security scanning, implement network policies for microsegmentation, and establish TLS certificate rotation verification.

Create cluster-level and namespace-level RBAC roles following least privilege, establish default-deny network policies per namespace, and restrict VM disk sources to approved registries through image pull policies. Deploy the Compliance Operator with ocp4-moderate scanning profiles and enable confidential computing for VMs processing sensitive data.

Frequent errors include overly permissive RBAC roles that allow unauthorized VM lifecycle operations. Not implementing default-deny network policies allows unrestricted inter-namespace VM communication. Deploying compliance scanning without remediation tracking gives false confidence in security posture.

activities.name: Tune VM Performance
activities.description: Optimize VM compute, memory, and I/O performance through advanced configuration.

narratives.name: Tuning VM Performance with CPU Pinning and NUMA Awareness
narratives.description: How to configure CPU pinning, NUMA topology awareness, huge pages, and I/O tuning to achieve near-bare-metal performance for VMs.

narrativeContexts.context: Establish performance baselines with default configurations, configure CPU pinning and NUMA awareness for compute optimization, allocate huge pages for memory-intensive workloads, and tune I/O through SR-IOV and storage configuration.

Configure dedicatedCpuPlacement for CPU pinning and deploy the NUMA Resources Operator with secondary scheduler for NUMA-aware scheduling. Allocate 2MB or 1GB huge pages on worker nodes, enable emulator thread isolation for guaranteed QoS, and configure SR-IOV, DPDK, or GPU/vGPU passthrough for I/O and compute-intensive workloads.

Common mistakes include configuring CPU pinning without NUMA awareness, which nullifies cache efficiency gains. Allocating huge pages without sufficient free memory on nodes causes OOM conditions. Cross-NUMA memory access from NUMA misalignment imposes a 10% or greater performance penalty.

activities.name: Configure GPU and Accelerator Access
activities.description: Set up PCI passthrough and vGPU sharing for GPU-accelerated VM workloads.

narratives.name: Enabling vGPU and PCI Passthrough for Accelerated Computing
narratives.description: How to configure PCI passthrough for dedicated GPU access or vGPU mediated devices for GPU sharing across VMs.

narrativeContexts.context: Configure PCI passthrough for dedicated GPU access or vGPU mediated devices for GPU sharing. Validate GPU performance against bare-metal benchmarks and establish resource quotas.

Enable IOMMU in BIOS and cluster configuration, then for PCI passthrough create HostDevice resources with node affinity rules, or for vGPU install the NVIDIA vGPU-KVM host driver and configure mediated device types supporting up to 16 vGPUs per physical GPU. Configure GPU resource quotas to prevent over-allocation and validate GPU access within guest OS against bare-metal performance benchmarks.

Critical risks in this area include not obtaining the NVIDIA vGPU-KVM host driver separately from NVIDIA, as Red Hat does not bundle it. Not enabling IOMMU causes passthrough configuration to fail silently. Over-allocating vGPUs per physical GPU degrades performance for all sharing VMs.

activities.name: Configure High Availability
activities.description: Establish VM availability mechanisms including eviction strategies, health checks, and remediation.

narratives.name: Configuring VM Eviction Strategies and Node Health Remediation
narratives.description: How to set LiveMigrate eviction strategies, configure machine health checks for automated node remediation, and distribute VMs across failure domains.

narrativeContexts.context: Set LiveMigrate eviction strategy for migratable VMs, configure machine health checks for automated node remediation, establish pod disruption budgets, and validate HA through failure simulation.

Set LiveMigrate as the default eviction strategy for migratable VMs and LiveMigrateIfPossible for VMs that may not always be migratable, ensuring RWX storage for all VMs requiring migration. Deploy machine health checks (IPI) or the Node Health Check Operator (non-IPI) for automated node remediation, and configure pod disruption budgets and anti-affinity rules to distribute critical VMs across failure domains.

Key pitfalls to avoid include using the None eviction strategy on migratable VMs, which causes unnecessary downtime during node maintenance. Single-node OpenShift does not support HA, live migration, or pod disruption budgets. Not configuring anti-affinity rules concentrates critical VMs on single failure domains.
